prompt: In the forward pass the MLP does 2.0 floating-point operations per parameter and the CNN 17.6. Why the difference?
hint: Count how many times one weight is used for one image.

choices.text: The CNN computes in float64
choices.why: Both run in float32; the counter counts operations, not bytes.

choices.text: A convolution weight is used at all 64 positions of the map
choices.why: Right. The filter slides over the 8 by 8 map, so each of its weights multiplies 64 times per image, where a dense weight multiplies once.

choices.text: The pooling layer has weights of its own that are counted
choices.why: Max pooling has no parameters; it picks the largest of four values.

choices.text: The counter includes the ReLUs as multiplications
choices.why: The counter adds up matrix products and convolutions; the MLP has a ReLU too and still comes out at 2.0.

prompt: A dense network of 1,000,000 parameters trains for one epoch on 50,000 examples. How many GFLOPs (billions of operations) does the 6 × N × D rule predict?
hint: Six, times the parameters, times the examples seen; then divide by a billion.

prompt: A colleague replaces a dense network of 2 million parameters with a convolutional one of 2 million, for 64 by 64 images, and keeps the same training budget because the parameter count is equal. What is wrong with the budget?
hint: The 6 × N × D rule assumes something about how often a weight is used.

choices.text: Nothing, since the 6 × N × D rule holds for every network whatever its layers
choices.why: It holds where each weight is used once per example. The CNN of this lesson did 52.4 operations per parameter per step, not 6.

choices.text: The convolutional network will be cheaper, because each of its layers holds fewer weights
choices.why: Smaller layers mean fewer parameters per layer, not less arithmetic: each weight is reused at every position.

choices.text: Its weights are reused at every position, so its arithmetic per image is far larger
choices.why: Right. On a 64 by 64 map a filter's weights work thousands of times per image, and the budget has to be counted from the arithmetic.

choices.text: Convolutions run only on graphics cards
choices.why: Lesson 11's CNN trained on this course's processor; a card is faster, not required.

prompt: The CNN did 198 times the MLP's arithmetic per training step, but took far fewer times as long. What explains the gap?
hint: What does a step cost that does not depend on the size of the matrices?

choices.text: The counter overstates what a convolution costs, counting each product twice
choices.why: The counter's numbers were checked by hand in this section; the arithmetic is real.

choices.text: PyTorch skips the multiplications by zero after a ReLU
choices.why: Dense routines multiply every entry, zeros included.

choices.text: Fixed overhead per step, which is most of the MLP's tiny step
choices.why: Right. Calling layers, checking shapes and allocating outputs cost the same for a small product as for a large one.

choices.text: The CNN was timed on smaller batches than the MLP, so each step had less to do
choices.why: Both were timed on the same batch of 32 digits.

prompt: Training in float32 with Adam, how many bytes per parameter do the weights, the gradients and the optimiser's state take together?
hint: Four bytes a number, and count the numbers kept per parameter.

choices.text: 4, the weight alone
choices.why: That is what the saved file holds; training keeps three more numbers per parameter.

choices.text: 8: the weight and its gradient
choices.why: Enough for plain SGD, which keeps no state. Adam keeps two averages more.

choices.text: 12, with one buffer for Adam
choices.why: One buffer is SGD with momentum. Adam keeps the average of the gradient and of its square.
Right: weight, gradient and Adam's two buffers, 4 bytes each. memory.py measured 153,128 + 153,128 + 306,256 for 38,282 parameters.

prompt: You double the batch size of a training run and change nothing else. Which part of the memory doubles?
hint: Which of the four does every example in the batch have its own copy of?

choices.text: The gradients, since twice as many examples contribute
choices.why: The gradient is averaged over the batch into one number per parameter; its size does not change.

choices.text: The activations saved for the backward pass
choices.why: Right: 18,992 bytes per example for the CNN, at a batch of 32 and at a batch of 1,077 alike.

choices.text: Adam's buffers
choices.why: They hold two numbers per parameter whatever the batch.

choices.text: The weights, which are copied per example
choices.why: One set of weights serves the whole batch; that is what a matrix product does.

prompt: A network of 3 million parameters, trained with Adam in float32 on 256 by 256 images, runs out of memory at a batch of 128. Which change frees the most memory?
hint: Compare 16 bytes per parameter with what each large image keeps for the backward pass.

choices.text: Replacing Adam with plain SGD
choices.why: It frees 8 bytes per parameter, 24 MB here, while the activations of 128 large images run to gigabytes.

choices.text: Batches of 32, accumulated four at a time
choices.why: Right. The activations grow with the batch and dominate at this image size; accumulation keeps the effective batch of 128.

choices.text: Storing the gradients in bfloat16 instead of float32
choices.why: That halves 12 MB of gradients and leaves the activations, the large part, untouched.

choices.text: Removing a tenth of the parameters from the last layers
choices.why: A tenth of 48 MB of parameter memory is small next to what the batch keeps.

prompt: Under mixed precision with bfloat16, why do the weights themselves stay in float32?
hint: Look at what precision.py printed for 1 + 0.001.

choices.text: bfloat16 cannot hold numbers as large as weights
choices.why: Its largest number is 3.39e+38, the same range as float32.

choices.text: A small update to a weight would round away in bfloat16
choices.why: Right. 1 + 0.001 comes back as 1 in bfloat16, so a weight kept there would stop moving.

choices.text: PyTorch's optimisers refuse bfloat16 tensors
choices.why: They accept them; the reason is the arithmetic of the update, not a refusal.

choices.text: So that the saved file stays compatible with lesson 9
choices.why: A state_dict can hold any type; the file has nothing to do with it.

prompt: What does a GradScaler protect a float16 training run from?
hint: precision.py's third test, 1e-6 × 1e-3.

choices.text: Weights growing past 65,504 and becoming inf
choices.why: The weights stay in float32 under mixed precision; the scaler acts on the gradients.

choices.text: Two runs with the same seed giving different numbers
choices.why: That is determinism, lesson 18's subject; the scaler does not touch it.

choices.text: Small gradients rounding to 0
choices.why: Right. It multiplies the loss before backward so they stay representable, and divides them back before the step.

choices.text: The step after 1 being too coarse for small updates
choices.why: That is bfloat16's weakness, and keeping the weights in float32 is what answers it.

prompt: In trap.py the training loss was 2.3230 in every epoch, yet the first-layer weights had moved by up to 0.2466. What happened?
hint: What does autocast keep for as long as its block lasts?

choices.text: bfloat16 rounded every update to zero
choices.why: Then the weights would not have moved; they did, because they are kept in float32.

choices.text: Each forward pass ran on cached copies of the initial weights
choices.why: Right. The block around the whole loop never ended, so the cache was never refreshed. One autocast per batch fixes it.

choices.text: A rate of 0.1 is too high for 16-bit arithmetic, so every step overshot
choices.why: mixed.py trained at 0.1 under autocast and reached 0.969.

choices.text: zero_grad does nothing inside an autocast block
choices.why: Gradients that piled up would make the loss jump about, not hold still to four decimals.

prompt: bfloat16 has the same largest number as float32 and a coarse step after 1; float16 is the other way round. In one word, what does float16 give up that bfloat16 keeps? ___
hint: Its largest number is 6.55e+04.

prompt: Put the lines of one accumulated step, over four pieces of 32, in order.
hint: The step reads .grad, and backward adds into it.
items: Compute the loss of one piece of 32
After the fourth piece, call opt.step()
Call opt.zero_grad() before the next four

prompt: A network with batch normalisation accumulates four pieces of 32. Is its gradient the gradient of a batch of 128?
hint: What does batch normalisation compute from the batch it is given?

choices.text: Yes, as accumulate.py showed for cnn.py
choices.why: cnn.py has no layer that looks across the batch; that is why the two agreed there.

choices.text: Yes, provided each of the four losses is divided by 4 before backward
choices.why: The division fixes the scale. It cannot fix statistics computed over 32 examples instead of 128.

choices.text: No: each piece is normalised with its own mean and variance
choices.why: Right. Four sets of statistics over 32 are not one set over 128, so the gradient differs. Layer normalisation has no such problem.

choices.text: No, because accumulating four pieces changes the learning rate
choices.why: With the division by 4 the scale is right; the difference is in the statistics.

prompt: `time python compare.py` printed a `user` time larger than its `real` time. How can a program use more time than it took?
hint: How many processors does the machine have?

choices.text: `user` adds up the time of every processor the program used
choices.why: Right. PyTorch split the products across four processors, so their times add up past the clock's.

choices.text: `user` includes the time the program spent waiting for other programs
choices.why: Waiting is in `real`, which runs on the clock; `user` counts only time spent computing.

choices.text: The shell's clock is less precise than the one inside the processor
choices.why: The difference is far larger than any imprecision; it is the four processors.

choices.text: `real` leaves out the time spent loading PyTorch
choices.why: `real` runs from start to finish, imports included.

prompt: A job is estimated at 4,083 card-hours. You rent 16 cards instead of 8. What happens to the bill?
hint: The bill is card-hours times the price.

choices.text: It halves, because the run takes half as long
choices.why: Half the days on twice the cards is the same number of card-hours.

choices.text: About the same, or a little more
choices.why: Right. The card-hours do not change, and exchanging gradients between more cards lowers the share of the peak kept.

choices.text: It doubles, because twice as many cards are rented
choices.why: They are rented for half as long, so the card-hours stay where they were.

choices.text: It falls, because the price per card drops with volume
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson's arithmetic, or in the price variable, says that.

prompt: In bill.py, KEPT falls from 0.40 to 0.20 and nothing else changes. By what factor do the card-hours multiply?
hint: KEPT divides the card-hours.

prompt: Going from 64 epochs to 128 raised the validation accuracy by 0.5 points. How much arithmetic did that doubling cost?
hint: Each line of the table has twice the arithmetic of the line above it.

choices.text: A tenth of the run so far
choices.why: 128 is twice 64, so the new epochs are as many as all the old ones.

choices.text: The same as the doubling from 4 epochs to 8 epochs
choices.why: That one added 4 epochs; this one added 64.

choices.text: As much as all the epochs before it together
choices.why: Right: 64 more epochs, for 0.5 points, where the doubling from 4 to 8 bought 7.5 for 4 epochs.

choices.text: Nothing, since the images were already in memory
choices.why: Memory is not arithmetic: every epoch runs the forward and backward passes again.

prompt: With the arithmetic of 1,077 images for 30 epochs, 270 images for 120 epochs reached 0.942 against the full run's 0.950. What does that support?
hint: Same amount of arithmetic, spent in two ways.

choices.text: 120 epochs is too many for any network, whatever the data
choices.why: On all 1,077 images, 128 epochs gave the best accuracy of the table.

choices.text: New examples are worth more than repeated passes
choices.why: Right. A small set gone over many times is learnt as itself rather than as digits, the overfitting of lesson 7.

choices.text: The arithmetic was not really equal
choices.why: 270 × 120 is 32,400 examples seen and 1,077 × 30 is 32,310: equal to within a batch.

choices.text: Smaller sets need a higher learning rate
choices.why: The rate was the same in both, and nothing in the run points at it.

prompt: Which of these stay the same size when the batch grows? Choose every one that does.

choices.text: The weights

choices.text: The gradients

choices.text: Adam's two buffers
choices.why: Two numbers per parameter, whatever the batch.

choices.text: The activations saved for backward
